As a result of the depth of weathering and steep slope conditions, the possibility of shallow slides should be considered. With the proper placement of access or operating roads, as well as cross drainage facilities, this problem would be eliminated.
The upper reservoir contains a saddle dike that is designed as a fuse plug, with a crest elevation that is two feet lower than that of the other two dams used to impound the reservoir. Overtopping of this structure would occur only if: (1) pumping did not cease when the reservoir reached full pool, or (2) the probable maximum flood occurred when the reservoir was full and the powerplant was out of service. In the event of overtopping of this dike, the embankment would be washed out, resulting in the temporary flooding of 200 to 500 acres of land (Duke Power Company, 1976b). Extensive erosion along the path of the floodwaters could occur, resulting in temporary increases in turbidity and siltation in the Lower Whitewater Falls region of the Whitewater River and in the Whitewater arm of Lake Jocassee.
Should overtopping of the upper reservoir occur, the waters entering Lake Jocassee would be handled by spillage from Jocassee Dam into Lake Keowee. Applicant (1976b) estimates that at most, Lake Jocassee would rise about 3.6 feet as a result of a total washout at Bad Creek, with water passing into Lake Keowee, raising the latter about 1.8 feet. This would presumably be in addition to any elevation caused by other inflows into the reservoirs occurring during a probable maximum flood.
Lake Jocassee is presently supporting a two-story fishery as described in Section 2.2.2.2. The existence of the coldwater habitat is dependent on the retention of a stratum of water of acceptable temperature and adequate dissolved oxygen (DO). The most critical period for retaining the coldwater stratum in Lake Jocassee is in late September to early October when combined temperature and DO conditions are least favorable.
Temperature and DO data for Lake Jocassee from 1973 to 1975 show a decrease in the trout habitat during late summer. Assessing the change from 1974 to 1975, Applicant has attributed the reduction in habitat thickness to operation of the Jocassee Pumped Storage Project in conjunction with heating of Lake Keowee by the Oconee Nuclear Power Plant, and natural causes. Applicant has stated that trout habitat has shifted downward in the lake from 1974 to 1975, due primarily to operation of the Jocassee facility.
